finding.claim: The caller's identity is taken directly from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified, with no session, signature or token check in this code. Any client can set the header to the name of a user who has grants on a file and then delete or rename that file. The header name suggests that a fronting proxy sets it after verification, but nothing in the repository strips or overwrites it, so this is exploitable whenever the app is reachable without such a proxy. The reverse proxy is outside the repository and I could not check it.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified on any request
finding.sink: ensure_allowed/is_allowed authorization decisions that gate `del STORE[fid]` (views.py:18) and the rename write `f["name"] = ...` (views.py:27)

trace.note: before_request sets g.user from the raw header with no verification
is_allowed only looks up resource['grants'][user], so a spoofed name that has a grant passes

finding.guards_checked: acl.py ensure_allowed/is_allowed check grants against the supplied user string, which is attacker-chosen. There is no authentication decorator, signature check or header stripping in the repository, and no proxy configuration is present. Missing header gives g.user=None, which has no grants and is denied, so the bypass requires the attacker to know or guess a granted username.

verdict.guard_found: acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed aborts 403 and views.py:25-26 checks is_allowed, both used correctly, but they trust the user string from the header. There is no header stripping, signature check or authentication in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every traced line is accurate (views.py:11 takes g.user raw from the header, views.py:17/25 pass it to acl.py:5, and the effects are at views.py:18/27), but whether a fronting proxy strips or overwrites X-Session-User-Verified is deployment-dependent and cannot be determined from these two files.
